name: Probabilistic index models (pim)
title: How often does the more-stressed bank pay out more?
what: A rank-based regression whose effect is a plain probability: “A beats B x% of the time.”
pick_line: Jared chose Engineering + Math (11-17). Top pick was: flag Q2 programs whose numbers contradict their text label.
data: Public filings (Fed DFAST results, FR Y-9C); descriptive only
one: Stress-test pre-tax income orders payouts; drawdown adds nothing beyond it.

left.sub: of the slope lost when 8 of 360 extreme rows are trimmed

right.sub: same trim: the effect barely moves (0.4675 → 0.4697)

findings.h: Stress-test pre-tax income orders payouts; drawdown adds nothing beyond it.
findings.t: A bank one IQR better on severely adverse pre-tax income has the higher payout/RWA 68% of the time (Holm p = 0.02).

chart.title: Chance the better-placed bank pays more

findings.h: It holds where the usual regression is fragile.
findings.t: Trimming the 8 most extreme payout ratios cuts the regression slope from −0.070 to −0.040. The PIM effect moves from 0.4675 to 0.4697.
findings.note: Bars computed from those numbers: 0.040/0.070, and (0.5−0.4697)/(0.5−0.4675).

chart.title: Effect kept after trimming 2% of rows

findings.h: Before 2020 stress showed up in dividends; after, maybe buybacks.
findings.t: Pre-2020 dividends: 36% per IQR (Holm p = 0.02); buybacks 49%. Post-2020 buybacks 44% (p = 0.034), which does not survive Holm (0.27).
findings.note: ✓ survives Holm · ? p < 0.05 but not after Holm.

findings.h: Benchmark vs ARDL and SARIMAX (11-17): ties ARDL, narrowly misses our bar.
findings.t: Held-out years 2016–25, share of same-year bank pairs ordered correctly. Payout/RWA: PIM with last year's payout 0.779 vs ARDL 0.775. Payout/NI: 0.688 vs ARDL 0.620, but 0.637 vs per-firm SARIMAX 0.657 on SARIMAX's rows.
findings.note: Pre-set rule: 'promising' needed PIM ≥ ARDL and ≥ SARIMAX on payout/NI. It beat ARDL (+0.068, 90% interval +0.030 to +0.101) but trailed SARIMAX by 0.020 (−0.095 to +0.042), so the Engineering and Math avenues did not start. Descriptive extra: ARDL's long-run drawdown effect loses 44% under the same 2% trim (OLS 43%, PIM under 2%).

chart.title: Pairs ordered correctly, payout/NI (0.5 = coin flip)

findings.h: Math avenue (11-17): firm-clustered errors are wider, and only pre-tax income keeps its result.
findings.t: Banks recur across years, so pim's default errors are too narrow. In a simulation at our design, nominal 95% intervals covered the truth 72% of the time; the new firm-clustered errors covered 91.7% (β = 0) and 91.8% (β = 0.5). The pre-set bar was 93.5–96.5%, so this is a miss. On the 11-16 table the errors are 1.5× wider (median). Pre-tax income still orders payouts (68%, Holm p = 0.005 over 29 rows). Drawdown alone (40%) and pre-2020 dividends (36%) no longer survive Holm.
findings.note: Holm over all 29 rows of the 11-16 table, for both kinds of error. Firm-block bootstrap: 95.0% / 93.2% (500 runs). The new errors still run about 9% narrow, so even the firm-clustered p-values are a little optimistic.

chart.title: 95% intervals that cover the truth (simulation, β = 0)

findings.h: Engineering avenue (11-17): exact match with pim; the numpy prototype is too slow, a Rust core is fast enough.
findings.t: All 24 fits and 29 coefficients match pim 2.0.4 to 3e-15 (β) and 7e-15 (SE). For 10,000 within-year permutations of the 360-row joint model, the pre-registered numpy prototype took 9.1 s against a bar of under 2 s: a miss. A Rust core, built afterwards and not pre-registered, took 0.29 s on 8 threads (0.57 s while the ecotraj run was using 6 cores; parity 5e-16). pim itself would take about 75 s.
findings.note: Speed measured on the shared box (load 4.4 after the ecotraj run ended; 11.2 s for numpy while it ran). Parity is exact either way.

findings.h: Build step 3 (11-23): a leave-one-firm-out jackknife fixes the coverage gap; the two planned fixes do not.
findings.t: Pre-registered rerun of the 11-17 design (40 firms × 13 years, 2,000 reps; SYNTHETIC). Firm SEs again cover 91.65% / 91.75%. The jackknife covers 94.20% (β = 0) and 94.15% (β = 0.5), inside the 93.5–96.5% band, so it becomes the default. Our dyadic CR2 adjustment adds only about one point (92.70% / 92.35%); the firm wild score bootstrap is worse (89.10% / 88.15%). Three options were tried and one passed.
findings.note: Computed; Monte Carlo SE about 0.5 points. The jackknife is still about 0.8 points below 95% and costs 40 refits (about 0.025 s per fit here). Scripts and the full table: runs/2026-11-23-build/pim/ and PREREG-P3.md Addendum 1.
